claims.claim: IDWR explains that a 1978 statute required holders of beneficial-use water rights, other than rights used solely for domestic purposes, to record them with IDWR, and that these statutory claims are affidavits that do not confirm the right. IDWR points owners to its Water Right & Adjudication Search to view water right records and documents.
claims.quotedLanguage: In 1978, a statute was enacted requiring persons with beneficial use rights (other than water rights used solely for domestic purposes) to record their water rights with IDWR. The purpose of the statute was to provide some means to make records of water rights for which there were previously no records. However, these records are merely affidavits of the water users, and do not result in a license, decree, or other confirmation of the water right. ... Use the Water Right & Adjudication Search to view water right records and associated documents.
claims.notes: Explains why a domestic-only well may have no claim on file. ⚠️ Do not extend this to 'domestic wells never have water right records' — some may have been decreed in an adjudication or permitted. Tell the reader to search the record, not to assume.

claims.claim: Idaho Code 42-1204 provides that easements, rights-of-way and real property owned by irrigation districts, Carey Act operating companies, nonprofit irrigation entities, lateral ditch associations and drainage districts are not subject to adverse possession, and that no one may block authorized personnel's free access to them.
claims.quotedLanguage: The easements, rights-of-way, or real property owned by irrigation districts, Carey act operating companies, nonprofit irrigation entities, lateral ditch associations, and drainage districts are not subject to adverse possession. (2) No person shall prevent free access of authorized personnel on such easements, rights-of-way, or other real property
claims.notes: ⚠️ RENUMBERED 2026: this was 42-1208 until 2026 ch. 109. Older documents and other sites cite 42-1208 — cite 42-1204. Chapter 12 index checked 2026-11-12; no future-dated version listed.

claims.claim: Idaho Code 42-1205 bars anyone from causing or permitting encroachments — including roads, utilities, fences, gates, pipelines, structures, landscaping, trees or vegetation — onto easements or rights-of-way of irrigation districts, lateral ditch associations and similar entities without that entity's written permission, which may not be unreasonably withheld; encroachments placed without permission that unreasonably or materially interfere must be removed or modified at the expense of whoever caused or permitted them.
claims.quotedLanguage: no person or entity shall cause or permit any encroachments onto the easements or rights-of-way, including any public or private roads, utilities, fences, gates, pipelines, structures, landscaping, trees, vegetation, or other construction or placement of objects, without the written permission of the irrigation district, Carey act operating company, nonprofit irrigation entity, lateral ditch association, or drainage district owning, operating, maintaining, or controlling the easement or right-of-way ... Such written permission shall not be unreasonably withheld. ... Encroachments of any kind placed in such easement or right-of-way, without such express written permission, shall be removed or modified, and the irrigation conduit, easement, or right-of-way shall be repaired or restored at the expense of the person or entity causing or permitting such encroachments
claims.notes: ⚠️ RENUMBERED 2026: formerly 42-1209. The removal duty is triggered 'in the event that any such encroachments unreasonably or materially interfere' and on request of the operator/owner — always keep both conditions. Never say whether a reader's fence or shed is an encroachment.

claims.claim: Idaho law prohibits anyone from engaging in the business or acting in the capacity of a real estate broker or salesperson in Idaho without an active Idaho real estate license, and unless an exemption applies, a single act within those definitions is enough to count as engaging in the business.
claims.quotedLanguage: No person shall engage in the business or act in the capacity of real estate broker or real estate salesperson in this state without an active Idaho real estate license therefor. Unless exempted from this chapter, any single act described within the definitions of "real estate broker" or "real estate salesperson" shall be sufficient to constitute "engaging in the business" within the meaning of this chapter.
claims.notes: One act is enough; do not say 'regularly' or 'in the business of'. Describe only; never say whether a given buyer needs a license.

claims.claim: Under Idaho's license law, a 'real estate broker' includes any person who, acting for another for compensation or the expectation of it, sells, lists, buys, negotiates or offers to do so for others; any person who represents to the public that they do these things; and any person who takes any part in procuring prospects or negotiating or closing a transaction calculated to result in those acts.
claims.quotedLanguage: "Real estate broker" means and includes: (a) Any person other than a real estate salesperson who, directly or indirectly, while acting for another for compensation or a promise or an expectation thereof, engages in any of the following: sells, lists, buys, or negotiates, or offers to sell, list, buy or negotiate the purchase, sale, option or exchange of real estate or any interest therein or business opportunity or interest therein for others; ... (c) Any person who represents to the public that the person is engaged in any of the activities in this subsection; (d) Any person who directly or indirectly engages in, directs, or takes any part in the procuring of prospects or in the negotiating or closing of any transaction which does or is calculated to result in any of the acts in this subsection; (e) A dealer in options as defined in this section.
claims.notes: Subsection is 54-2004(39) in the current text. IREC Guideline 2 (rev. 2018) still cites it as 54-2004(36) — numbering has shifted; cite (39) or no subsection number.

claims.claim: Idaho's license law defines a 'dealer in options' as anyone who takes, obtains or uses options to purchase real property for another or others, whether or not the options are in their own name and whether or not title passes through them; a dealer in options falls within the definition of real estate broker.
claims.quotedLanguage: "Dealer in options" means any person, firm, partnership, association or corporation who shall directly or indirectly take, obtain or use options to purchase, exchange, lease option or lease purchase real property or any interest therein for another or others whether or not the options shall be in his or its name and whether or not title to the property shall pass through the name of the person, firm, partnership, association or corporation
claims.notes: Subsection 54-2004(20). Pair with vb-broker-definition-acting-for-others for the 'falls within broker' half (54-2004(39)(e)).

claims.claim: An Idaho real estate license is not required to buy, option, exchange or sell an interest in real property for a person's own account or use, or for an owner to dispose of its own property; but the exceptions may not be used to evade the license law, and any attempt to do so is treated as unlicensed practice.
claims.quotedLanguage: an Idaho real estate license is not required for the following: (a) The purchase, option, exchange or sale of any interest in real property, or business opportunity for a person’s own account or use; (b) The acquisition, exchange or other disposition of any interest in real property or business opportunity by its owner ... (4) Exceptions to licensure shall not be used in any way to evade the purposes of this chapter. Any such attempt to evade this chapter shall be considered the unlicensed and unlawful practice of real estate.
claims.notes: This is why a direct buyer purchasing for itself needs no license. State the exception and the anti-evasion clause together.

claims.claim: Acting as a real estate broker or salesperson in Idaho without a license is a misdemeanor; on conviction a natural person faces a fine of up to $5,000, up to one year in county jail, or both, and an LLC or corporation a fine of up to $10,000. A court may also assess civil penalties of up to $5,000 against a person and $10,000 against an LLC or corporation.
claims.quotedLanguage: Any person acting as a real estate broker or real estate salesperson within the meaning of this chapter without a license as herein provided shall be guilty of a misdemeanor and, upon conviction thereof, if a natural person, be punished by a fine of not to exceed five thousand dollars ($5,000) or by imprisonment in the county jail for a term not to exceed one (1) year, or by both such fine and imprisonment in the discretion of the court; or if a limited liability company or corporation, by a fine of not to exceed ten thousand dollars ($10,000). Additionally, the court may assess a civil penalty against a natural person in an amount not to exceed five thousand dollars ($5,000) and against a limited liability company or corporation in an amount not to exceed ten thousand dollars ($10,000).
claims.notes: Penalties fall on the unlicensed actor, not the seller. Do not imply a seller is exposed to them.

claims.claim: An Idaho real estate licensee who buys or sells an interest in real property for personal use or any other purpose, or acquires or intends to acquire an interest or option, must disclose in writing to the other party, no later than when the purchase and sale agreement is presented, that they hold an active Idaho license.
claims.quotedLanguage: A licensee shall disclose in writing to any buyer or seller no later than at the time of presentation of the purchase and sale agreement that the licensee holds an active Idaho real estate license, if the licensee directly, indirectly, or through a third party, sells or purchases an interest in real property for personal use or any other purpose; or acquires or intends to acquire any interest in real property or any option to purchase real property.
claims.notes: Applies to ACTIVE Idaho licensees only. Covers purchases 'through a third party' — e.g. an entity.

claims.claim: When an Idaho broker or sales associate handles an offer to purchase real property, the license law requires it to be in writing and to state the actual form and amount of the earnest money and include a provision for dividing earnest money retained as forfeited payment if the transaction does not close.
claims.quotedLanguage: The broker or sales associate shall make certain that all offers to purchase real property or any interest therein are in writing and contain all of the following specific terms, provisions and statements: ... (b) The actual form and amount of the consideration received as earnest money; ... (e) A provision for division of earnest money retained by any person as forfeited payment should the transaction not close;
claims.notes: Duty is on the BROKER/SALES ASSOCIATE. A direct sale with no licensee is not governed by this section — say so plainly.

claims.claim: Under Idaho's license law, money is not treated as entrusted to a broker when the parties have instructed the broker in writing to transfer it to a third party such as a title, escrow or trust company and the broker then has no right to control its safekeeping or disposition.
claims.quotedLanguage: moneys or property shall not be considered entrusted to the broker or to any licensee representing the broker when the parties to the transaction have instructed the broker or its licensees, in writing, to transfer such moneys or property to a third party, including, but not limited to, a title, an escrow or a trust company if upon transfer, the broker or its licensees have no right to exercise control over the safekeeping or disposition of said moneys or property.
claims.notes: Broker-side rule. Use only to explain that earnest money held at a title or escrow company sits with that company, not with a broker.

claims.claim: It is unlawful to engage in, carry on, or purport to carry on the business of an escrow agency in or from Idaho without a license under the Idaho Escrow Act, and the Act applies to any escrow transaction for the sale or transfer of property located in Idaho.
claims.quotedLanguage: It shall be unlawful for any person to directly or indirectly engage in or carry on, or purport to engage in or carry on, the business of, or act in the capacity of, an escrow agency in or from Idaho without first obtaining a license under this chapter. (2) The requirements of this chapter shall also apply to any escrow transaction effecting the sale, transfer, encumbrance or lease to another person of any real or personal property located in Idaho.
claims.notes: Read with the 30-905 exemptions; licensed title agents, lawyers, banks and brokers acting incidentally are exempt.

claims.claim: The Idaho Escrow Act's licensing requirements do not apply to title insurance companies holding a certificate of authority, or to title insurance agents holding a title insurance agent license, issued by the Idaho Department of Insurance.
claims.quotedLanguage: The requirements of this chapter do not apply to: ... (3) Title insurance companies having a valid certificate of authority, and title insurance agents having a valid license as a title insurance agent, issued by the Idaho department of insurance;
claims.notes: This is why a title company's credential to check is a Department of Insurance license, while a standalone escrow company's is a Department of Finance license. Ten other exemptions exist (lawyers, banks, brokers etc.) — do not say title agents are the only exempt group.

claims.claim: Acting as an escrow agency in Idaho without the required license, unless exempt, is a felony and carries a civil penalty of up to $5,000 per violation.
claims.quotedLanguage: Any person, except a person exempt under section 30-905, Idaho Code, who engages in activity as an escrow agency without first obtaining a license in accordance with this chapter, shall be guilty of a felony. Such person is also subject to a civil penalty in an amount no greater than five thousand dollars ($5,000) for each violation of this chapter or rule or order thereunder, in addition to other sanctions allowed by law.

claims.claim: No one may act in Idaho as an agent for a title insurer without a license from the Director of the Idaho Department of Insurance, and a title insurance agent's license is required for each county for which policies are written.
claims.quotedLanguage: A title insurer shall not allow or permit any person, firm, association or corporation to act as its agent in relation to the issuance of any certificate, title insurance policy, or other underwriting contract unless such person, firm, association or corporation shall first have obtained a title insurance agent’s license for each county for which policies are to be written from the director of the department of insurance. No person, firm, association or corporation shall act within this state as such agent for any title insurer without first having obtained a license from the director of insurance and filed a bond or cash deposit in lieu thereof as required herein.
claims.notes: County-by-county license: an agent licensed for one county is not thereby licensed for Ada. Do not say 'must be licensed in Ada' for a given file — say the license is per county.

claims.claim: In enacting the Consumer Foreclosure Protection Act, the Idaho Legislature found that some persons and businesses defraud homeowners of their title, equity or other value under the guise of stopping or postponing a foreclosure sale, and set notice requirements for contracts made during the foreclosure period, while directing that the chapter not inhibit transactions with legitimate lenders and investors.
claims.quotedLanguage: The legislature finds that some persons and businesses are engaging in patterns of conduct that defraud innocent homeowners of their title, equity interest, or other value in residential dwellings under the guise of stopping or postponing a foreclosure sale. The legislature also finds this activity to be contrary to the public policy of this state and therefore establishes notice requirements governing contracts or agreements entered into during the foreclosure period. The legislature further finds that the provisions of this chapter shall be construed in such a manner that it does not inhibit transactions with legitimate lenders and investors.

claims.claim: During the foreclosure period described in Idaho Code 45-1506, any contract with the record owner involving the transfer of an interest in residential real property subject to foreclosure must be in writing and accompanied by a statutory notice in at least 12-point boldface type, which warns that some individuals or businesses may say they can 'save' a home from foreclosure, that a 'rescue' plan may cost the owner valuable equity, and that the owner should consult an attorney or financial professional, and points to HUD's list of approved housing counselors who provide free information.
claims.quotedLanguage: During the foreclosure period described in section 45-1506, Idaho Code, any contract or agreement with the owner or owners of record that involves the transfer of any interest in residential real property, as defined in section 45-525 (5)(b), Idaho Code, subject to foreclosure must be in writing and must be accompanied by the following notice in at least 12-point boldface type: ... Some individuals or businesses may say they can "save" your home from foreclosure. You should be cautious about such claims. It is important that you understand all the terms of a plan to "rescue" you from mortgage foreclosure and how it will affect you. It may result in your losing valuable equity that you may have in your home. If possible, you should consult with an attorney or financial professional to find out what other options you may have. ... HUD maintains on its website a list of approved housing counselors who can provide free information to assist homeowners with financial problems.
claims.notes: TRAP: the statutory notice text says 'five (5) days' to rescind, but the operative section 45-1603 says five BUSINESS days. Use 45-1603's wording for the right itself. A Spanish-language form is required when the deal was negotiated in Spanish (45-1602(2)).

claims.claim: An Idaho owner whose property is in foreclosure may cancel any contract relating to that property entered into during the foreclosure period within five business days of entering into it, by written notice to the other parties in any form showing an intent not to be bound; no funds or interest in the property may be transferred until the five days have passed.
claims.quotedLanguage: any person whose property is in foreclosure as described in section 45-1505, Idaho Code, has the right to cancel or rescind any and all contracts or agreements relating to such property entered into during the foreclosure period within five (5) business days of entering into such contract or agreement. Neither funds nor an interest in the property shall be transferred or transferable until the five (5) days have passed. (2) Cancellation occurs when such person gives written notice of cancellation to all other parties to the contract. Notice of cancellation need not take any particular form and, however expressed, is effective if it indicates the intention not to be bound by the contract.
claims.notes: Business days, from entering into the contract. Mailed notice effective on deposit; certified mail = conclusive proof (45-1603(3)). Never tell a reader whether their property is 'in foreclosure' for this purpose.

claims.claim: Idaho's Consumer Foreclosure Protection Act does not apply to regulated lenders, banks and similar chartered institutions, licensed mortgage lenders and brokers, their employees and agents acting in that capacity, or close family members of the owner.
claims.quotedLanguage: The provisions of this chapter shall not apply to: (1) Regulated lenders, as defined in section 28-41-301, Idaho Code; (2) Any person licensed or chartered under the laws of any state or of the United States as a bank, trust company, savings and loan association, credit union, or industrial loan company. ... (3) Mortgage lenders and mortgage brokers licensed under the Idaho residential mortgage practices act, sections 26-31-101 et seq., Idaho Code; (4) Employees and agents of the organizations specified in subsections (1), (2) and (3) of this section, when acting within the scope of such employment or agency; and (5) Family member or members of the owner or owners of record of any interest in residential real property subject to foreclosure.
claims.notes: Investors and cash buyers are NOT in the exclusion list. Do not state that as 'applies to cash buyers' application to a reader — just that the excluded groups are these.

claims.claim: A violation of Idaho's Consumer Foreclosure Protection Act makes the violator liable for penalties and damages under the Idaho Consumer Protection Act (chapter 6, title 48), in addition to any other penalty provided by law.
claims.quotedLanguage: In addition to any other penalty provided by law, any person who violates the provisions of this chapter shall be liable for penalties and damages in accordance with chapter 6, title 48, Idaho Code.
claims.notes: Title 48 ch. 6 sections themselves not researched; do not describe their remedies.

claims.claim: The Idaho Real Estate Commission's Guideline 18 states its interpretation that an option holder is not an owner and may not broker the property without a license, and that whether or not an investor holds an option, the investor may be engaged in unlicensed practice if they list, sell or negotiate the sale of property they do not own, or procure buyers for it. The Commission states that the guideline is not a new law but an agency interpretation of existing law.
claims.quotedLanguage: Because an option holder is not an owner of the property, he may not list, sell, negotiate, procure buyers for, or otherwise broker that property unless he has a license. ... Whether an Investor has an option to purchase or not, he may be engaged in Unlicensed Practice if he lists, sells, or negotiates the sale of property he does not own, or if he procures buyers for property that he does not own. ... This guideline is not a new law but is an agency interpretation of existing law.
claims.notes: Agency INTERPRETATION, not statute — always attribute to the Commission and say it is interpretation. Do not use the words 'wholesaling' or 'assignment': the guideline does not use them and no Idaho statute does. Never say what this site's company does.

claims.claim: The Idaho Real Estate Commission interprets 'procuring prospects' in the broker definition to include any marketing or advertising designed to attract the attention of buyers or sellers.
claims.quotedLanguage: The Commission interprets procuring prospects to include any marketing or advertising designed to attract the attention of buyers or sellers.
claims.notes: Agency interpretation (Guideline 2, rev. May 2018). Pair with 54-2004(39)(d).

claims.claim: The Idaho Real Estate Commission's License Lookup lets consumers confirm that an agent or brokerage is licensed in Idaho and see any formal disciplinary actions taken against an agent within the last five years.
claims.quotedLanguage: Consumers can utilize the Commission’s License Lookup application to ensure an agent or brokerage are licensed to practice real estate in Idaho. Additionally, consumers can see any formal disciplinary actions taken against an agent within the last five years.
claims.notes: The Commission is now administered through DOPL (dopl.idaho.gov/rec); the old irec.idaho.gov is not the current home.

claims.claim: The Idaho Real Estate Commission investigates complaints involving, among other things, dishonest or dishonorable dealings, failure to account for money or property, misrepresentation and unlicensed practice; it cannot enforce or cancel purchase and sale agreements, award damages or order the return of earnest money.
claims.quotedLanguage: The Commission investigates complaints against licensees involving: ... Dishonest or Dishonorable Dealings Failure to Account for Money or Property ... Misrepresentation ... Unlicensed Practice ... The Commission is NOT empowered to enforce, modify, rescind or cancel listing agreements, purchase and sale agreements, or any other contract; compel the payment of money, award damages, or render a judgment in your favor; order the return of earnest money;

claims.claim: The Idaho Real Estate Commission treats earnest money disputes as civil matters: it cannot decide them or order earnest money released, and it points consumers to the Idaho State Bar to find an attorney.
claims.quotedLanguage: Earnest Money Disputes Disputes over earnest money are civil matters. The Commission is not empowered to decide earnest money disputes or order the release of earnest money. The Idaho State Bar can help you find an attorney.

claims.claim: According to the Idaho Real Estate Commission, the Idaho Department of Finance has jurisdiction over escrow companies and the Idaho Department of Insurance regulates title insurance providers.
claims.quotedLanguage: Escrow Companies The Idaho Department of Finance has jurisdiction over escrow companies. ... Title Insurance The Idaho Department of Insurance regulates insurance providers in Idaho.

claims.claim: The Idaho Real Estate Commission warns that hackers try to divert closing payments to their own accounts by sending last-minute wiring instructions that differ from those provided by the settlement agent or real estate agent.
claims.quotedLanguage: A recent trend in real estate transactions involves hackers attempting to divert payments meant for the settlement agent to their own accounts by providing last minute wiring instructions different than those provided by the settlement agent or your real estate agent.
claims.notes: The page's 'nearly $1 billion in 2017' FBI figure is secondhand and dated — do not use it.

claims.claim: The Idaho Secretary of State's Business Search at sosbiz.idaho.gov lets anyone look up business information and registered agents; a registered agent must have a physical street address in Idaho (no P.O. box) and be an Idaho resident or a business entity authorized to do business in Idaho.
claims.quotedLanguage: Use the Business Search to lookup business information, registered agents, and more at sosbiz.idaho.gov. ... To be a registered agent in Idaho, you must: Have a physical street address in Idaho (no P.O. boxes) Be available during normal business hours Be either: An individual who lives in Idaho, or A business entity authorized to do business in Idaho
claims.notes: SOSBiz search results page is JavaScript-driven and could not be cached; do NOT list specific fields (status, formation date, officers) the search shows. Say only 'business information and registered agents'.

claims.claim: The Idaho Secretary of State says a certificate of existence is not required to do business in Idaho and warns of scam websites or mailings that suggest one is necessary.
claims.quotedLanguage: A certificate of existence is not required to do business in Idaho. Scam websites or mailings may try to indicate a certificate is necessary and offer to provide one at a high markup.
claims.notes: Means a buyer cannot be expected to produce one; the free search is the check.

claims.claim: The Idaho Department of Insurance's title insurance page offers a 'Find a Title Agent / Company' search and a title insurance specialist contact, and states that title insurance is not required in Idaho, though a lender may require a lender's policy.
claims.quotedLanguage: Title Insurance is not required in the state of Idaho. However, your lender may require you to purchase a Title Insurance Lender's Policy to protect their interests. Find a Title Agent / Company
claims.notes: Link target is an external NAIC lookup not cached; state only that the DOI page offers the search.

claims.claim: The Federal Trade Commission warns that mortgage relief scammers may try to get homeowners to transfer the deed to them, and that a homeowner who transfers the deed is not likely to get it back; it adds that transferring the deed does not transfer the mortgage.
claims.quotedLanguage: Scammers may try to convince you to transfer the deed to your home to them. The deed is the legal document that proves who owns the home. If you transfer the deed, you’re not likely to get it back. ... Transferring the deed does not transfer the mortgage, so you’ll still owe payments on your mortgage loan.
claims.notes: Federal consumer guidance, not Idaho law.

claims.claim: The FTC describes 'equity-skimming' schemes in which a homeowner is told they can get the home back later, or is tricked into selling for much less than similar homes, and the scammer then rents out the home while the lender proceeds with foreclosure, leaving the homeowner still responsible for the mortgage.
claims.quotedLanguage: Scammers say: “If you sell us your home, we’ll help you. You can get your home back once you’re on your feet again.” Others trick you into selling them your home for cash for much lower than the selling price of similar homes in your neighborhood. ... Once you sell your home to the scammer (and transfer the deed), they simply rent out the home and pocket the rent money while your lender goes ahead with the foreclosure. You lose your home — and you’re still responsible for the unpaid mortgage.
claims.notes: The FTC itself names 'selling ... for cash for much lower' as a scam pattern. Quote it straight; do not soften it — this page is about checking cash buyers, us included.

claims.claim: The FTC warns homeowners never to pay a company upfront for promises of mortgage relief, and notes that scammers may want payment only by cashier's check, wire transfer or a mobile payment app because such payments are hard to recover.
claims.quotedLanguage: Never pay a company upfront for promises to help you get relief on paying your mortgage. ... Scammers may want you to pay only by cashier’s check, wire transfer , or a mobile payment app . Scammers like you to pay this way because it’s hard to get your money back.
claims.notes: Mortgage-relief context. Apply only to 'a buyer or company asking the seller to pay money'.

claims.claim: Idaho requires all taxable real, personal and operating property to be assessed annually at market value for assessment purposes as of 12:01 a.m. on January 1 of the year in which the taxes are levied, except as otherwise provided.
claims.quotedLanguage: All real, personal and operating property subject to property taxation must be assessed annually at market value for assessment purposes as of 12:01 a.m. of the first day of January in the year in which such property taxes are levied, except as otherwise provided.
claims.notes: This is the ASSESSMENT date, not the lien date. 63-205 says nothing about liens — do not cite it for the lien. The lien is 63-206 (real property; existing claim ln-property-tax-first-lien-perpetual) and the January 1 lien date for real property is stated by the Ada County Assessor (pt-ada-lien-date-jan-1).

claims.claim: The Ada County Assessor states that the lien date for real property and most personal property is January 1.
claims.quotedLanguage: The lien date for real property and most personal property is January 1.
claims.notes: Same cached page as existing claim ada-assessment-market-value-jan-1, whose quotedLanguage carries only the market-value sentence; this claim puts the lien-date sentence itself on record so it can be quoted. County guidance, not statute — attribute to the Assessor.

claims.claim: Idaho property taxes are due in full by December 20 of the year they are levied, or may be paid in two halves: the first by December 20, with a grace period to June 20 for the second half if the first half is paid in full.
claims.quotedLanguage: All property taxes extended on the property and operating property rolls shall be due and payable in full to the tax collector without late charges and interest on or before December 20 of the year in which the property taxes are levied. The property taxes may be paid in full or paid in two (2) halves, the first half on or before December 20 with a grace period extending to June 20 for the second half if the first half is totally paid.
claims.notes: FUTURE-DATING CHECKED 2026-11-12: last amendment 2026 ch. 20 (H0594), which the Legislature's bill page shows as 'Effective: 07/01/2026' — already in force, and the section page shows no [EFFECTIVE ...] alternate version. H0594 concerned late charges/interest and their apportionment; the December 20 / June 20 structure is the text displayed now.

claims.claim: If the first half of Idaho property tax is not fully paid by December 20, or the second half by June 20, late charges and interest are assessed.
claims.quotedLanguage: If the first one-half (1/2) is not totally paid on or before December 20, late charges as defined in section 63-201, Idaho Code, and interest as provided in section 63-1001, Idaho Code, shall be assessed. ... If the second one-half (1/2) is not totally paid on or before June 20, late charges as defined in section 63-201, Idaho Code, and interest as provided in section 63-1001, Idaho Code, shall be assessed.
claims.notes: The statute defines the charges by cross-reference; the percentages on the page come from the Ada County Treasurer (pt-ada-late-charge-and-interest-rates), not from this section.

claims.claim: The Ada County Treasurer explains that values assessed as of January 1 are used for taxes billed in November and due in December of the same year, with primary-roll bills mailed by the fourth Monday in November.
claims.quotedLanguage: Property values in Idaho are assessed as of January 1 and billed and due later that same year. For example, values assessed on January 1, are used to determine your taxes that will be billed in November and due in December. ... the Treasurer’s Office to prepare the current year’s Primary Roll tax bills to be mailed out by the fourth Monday in November.
claims.notes: The practical consequence for a seller: a sale that closes before late November closes before that year's bill exists. Stating that consequence is arithmetic on these dates, not a rule about who pays. ⚠️ The same FAQ page labels the installments '1st half of 2025 taxes (January – June 2025)' and '2nd half … (July – December 2025)'. That is the Treasurer's description of the installments, NOT a statutory proration rule between buyer and seller — never cite it as one.

claims.claim: The Ada County Treasurer states that a missed December installment draws a 2% late charge plus interest at 1% per month from the following January 1, and that payments are applied to the oldest tax balance first.
claims.quotedLanguage: If the December installment is not paid by the deadline, a 2% late charge is added, along with interest at 1% per month beginning January 1 following the due date. ... Payments are applied to the oldest tax balance first.
claims.notes: County statement of current practice. The statutory definitions are in 63-201 and 63-1001, which were NOT read for this page — attribute the figures to the Treasurer. 'Oldest balance first' matters to a seller with arrears: a payment intended for the current year may go to an older delinquency.

claims.claim: The Ada County Treasurer says a consolidated property tax bill reflects the homestead exemption, which can also be checked on the Assessor's website.
claims.quotedLanguage: Your consolidated property tax bill will reflect your homestead exemption, or your can view that information on the Assessor’s website.
claims.notes: 'your can view' is the county's typo, kept verbatim.

claims.claim: Idaho's homeowner's (homestead) property-tax exemption is the lesser of the first $125,000 of the homestead's market value for assessment purposes or 50% of that value; the text displayed on 2026-11-12 reflects the section's latest amendment (2026 ch. 236, H0843), which took effect retroactively to January 1, 2026, and no later-dated version is displayed.
claims.quotedLanguage: For each tax year, the first one hundred twenty-five thousand dollars ($125,000) of the market value for assessment purposes of the homestead as that term is defined in section 63-701, Idaho Code, or fifty percent (50%) of the market value for assessment purposes of the homestead as that term is defined in section 63-701, Idaho Code, whichever is the lesser, shall be exempt from property taxation.
claims.notes: 🎯 RESOLVES red-team FINDING 1 (verificationFlag EFFECTIVE_DATE_UNCONFIRMED on existing claim id-homeowners-tax-exemption-125k). Chain of evidence, all cached 2026-11-12: (1) the section page shows the 2026 ch. 236 amendment as the latest and carries no [EFFECTIVE …] alternate text (re-fetched today and compared: byte-identical to the 2026-09-09 cache); (2) the Legislature's H0843 bill page reads 'Signed by Governor on March 31, 2026 … Session Law Chapter 236 … Effective: Retroactive to 01/01/2026' (entity-encoded, so it is cited but not quoted); (3) the printed bill's SECTION 2 declares an emergency and makes the act effective 'retroactively to January 1, 2026' (claim pt-h0843-retroactive-jan-1-2026); (4) the Statement of Purpose says the change was the removal of proration; (5) the Ada County Assessor independently states 50% up to a maximum of $125,000. No other 2026 bill amending 63-602G passed (H0885 and H0961 remained in committee per the 2026 legislation index). This duplicates the existing claim's quote ON PURPOSE because the existing claim is held back at render by its flag; a reviewer may instead clear that flag and swap ids. ⚠️ Still a TERMINOLOGY TRAP: not 55-1003 (creditor homestead, $175,000).

claims.claim: House Bill 843 of 2026, which amended Idaho Code 63-602G, declared an emergency and took effect on passage and approval and retroactively to January 1, 2026.
claims.quotedLanguage: AMENDING SECTION 63-602G, IDAHO CODE, TO REVISE PROVI- ... An emergency existing therefor, which emergency is hereby ... declared to exist, this act shall be in full force and effect on and after its ... passage and approval, and retroactively to January 1, 2026.
claims.notes: Quoted from the pdftotext extraction of the PRINTED bill (data/idaho/raw/extracted/dea662824b1ba20c.txt). The PDF carries line numbers in the margin, so the quote is split on each printed line; each fragment is verbatim. The bill page records no amendment between printing and passage (passed House 68-0-2 and Senate 32-0-3 as printed). The enrolled session-law PDF was not separately retrieved. pdftotext does not render strike-through, so struck and new text appear run together in the extraction — never quote statute text from this PDF; quote the section page.

claims.claim: The sponsor's Statement of Purpose for H0843 says the bill removes provisions requiring the homeowner's exemption to be prorated when a property's eligibility status changes during the tax year.
claims.quotedLanguage: The bill removes provisions requiring the exemption to be prorated when the eligibility status of a property changes during the tax year.
claims.notes: MEDIUM because the SOP carries its own disclaimer: it is 'prepared by a proponent of the bill' and is 'neither intended as an expression of legislative intent'. Use only to explain WHAT changed, and pair with the operative statute text (pt-homestead-exemption-not-prorated).

claims.claim: Under Idaho Code 63-602G(5) as now in force, the full homeowner's exemption applies as of January 1 of the tax year in which a complete application is submitted and approved, the exemption is not prorated, and the application for the current year is due by the end of the county's business hours on the last business day of the year.
claims.quotedLanguage: The full amount of the exemption allowed by this section shall be in effect as of January 1 of the tax year in which a complete application is submitted and approved, and shall be taken before the reductions in taxes provided in sections 63-701 through 63-710, Idaho Code, are applied. The exemption allowed by this section shall not be prorated. In order to receive the exemption for the current tax year, the homeowner shall make application on or before the end of the county's normal business hours on the last business day of the year.
claims.notes: ⚠️ This is about the EXEMPTION, not about splitting the tax bill between buyer and seller — that split is contractual and no statute read for this page sets it. Before 2026 the section's (5)(b) prorated taxes by day count on an eligibility change (visible in the printed H0843); that text is gone as of 1 Jan 2026. Older secondary material describing day-count proration of the exemption is now stale.

claims.claim: An Idaho homeowner need apply for the exemption only once so long as the owner received it the previous year on a valid application and still occupies the same homestead as a primary dwelling.
claims.quotedLanguage: An owner need make application for the exemption described in subsection (1) of this section only once, as long as all of the following conditions are met: ... The owner or beneficiary, partner, member or shareholder, as appropriate, still occupies the same homestead for which the owner made application.
claims.notes: Pairs with existing ada-homeowners-exemption-deadline and pt-ada-new-owner-must-apply: a sale breaks the 'same owner, same homestead' condition, so the buyer applies afresh.

claims.claim: The Ada County Assessor states that an approved homestead exemption lasts as long as the owner owns and occupies the property, and that if the property is sold the new owner must file an application.
claims.quotedLanguage: When the application is approved, the exemption is permanent as long as one owns and occupies the property. If the property is sold, the new owner must file an application with the assessor’s office.
claims.notes: County guidance. Also on the page: reapplication is needed on 'ownership updates such as adding or removing owners from a property, or properties being transferred into trusts' — relevant to an owner who deeds into a trust before selling.

claims.claim: Idaho allows a homestead exemption to be claimed after January 1 on a property not already exempt; if that taxpayer is also receiving an exemption on a separate property from a prior tax year, the exemption on the separate property is removed the following tax year.
claims.quotedLanguage: Nothing in this paragraph shall prohibit a taxpayer from claiming a homestead exemption after January 1 for a property that is not already subject to the homestead exemption, provided any claim for an exemption is consistent with the requirements of subsection (2)(c)(iii) of this section. If a taxpayer claims a homestead exemption after January 1 and is receiving a homestead exemption claimed on a separate property in a prior tax year, the exemption on such separate property shall be removed the following tax year.
claims.notes: ⚠️ DISCREPANCY: the Ada Assessor's page (cached 2026-09-09) says exemptions are not removed in the current assessment year if the owner qualified on Jan 1, 'unless said property owner(s) were to apply and qualify for an exemption on a different property by the second Monday in July within the same assessment year' — which reads as removal in the SAME year. The statute says 'the following tax year'. The page states only the statute and sends the reader to the Assessor. Do not reconcile the two in prose.

claims.claim: A taxpayer first discovered to have claimed more than one Idaho homestead exemption owes a penalty equal to the recovered property tax, in addition to the recovery, and a further violation within seven years is a misdemeanor.
claims.quotedLanguage: Upon the first instance of a taxpayer being discovered to have claimed more than one (1) homestead exemption, the taxpayer shall be subject to a penalty, payable to the county treasurer, in an amount equal to the amount of property tax recovered pursuant to subparagraph (ii) of this paragraph, which shall be paid in addition to such recovery amount. ... Any subsequent violation within seven (7) years of an instance pursuant to subparagraph (iii) of this paragraph shall be a misdemeanor
claims.notes: Relevant to an owner who buys and occupies a new home before the old one sells. Describe the statute only; never tell a reader whether their own situation is a double claim.

claims.claim: An Idaho homestead that qualified the previous year keeps its exemption through the year of the owner's death and the following tax year, provided it remains part of the owner's estate; after that, the new owner must reapply and qualify.
claims.quotedLanguage: A homestead that previously qualified for exemption under this section in the preceding year shall not lose such qualification due to the owner's, beneficiary's, partner's, member's or shareholder's death during the year of the owner's, beneficiary's, partner's, member's or shareholder's death and the tax year immediately following such death, provided that the homestead continues to be a part of the owner's, beneficiary's, partner's, member's or shareholder's estate. After such time, the new owner shall reapply to receive the exemption pursuant to this section and shall meet the qualification criteria contained in this section.
claims.notes: The condition is that the homestead 'continues to be a part of the … estate'. Do not say the exemption survives a sale out of the estate.

claims.claim: To claim Idaho's property tax reduction a person must have applied for the homeowner's exemption, own the homestead on January 1 or before April 15 of the first claim year, have lawful presence, and on January 1 fall in a listed category such as being 65 or older, a widow or widower, blind, or disabled as the statute defines.
claims.quotedLanguage: "Claimant" means a person who has filed an application under section 63-602G, Idaho Code, and has filed a claim under the provisions of sections 63-701 through 63-710, Idaho Code. Except as provided in section 63-702 (2), Idaho Code, on January 1 or before April 15 of the year in which the claimant first filed a claim on the homestead in question, a claimant must be an owner of the homestead, a claimant must have lawful presence in the United States pursuant to section 67-7903, Idaho Code, and on January 1 of said year a claimant must be: ... Not less than sixty-five (65) years old; or ... A widow or widower; or ... Blind.
claims.notes: Income limits are published annually by the State Tax Commission (63-705) and are NOT stated on the page. The full category list also includes certain fatherless/motherless children, disabled persons recognised by named agencies, disabled veterans, and former POWs/hostages; the page summarises rather than lists eligibility rules for a reader's own case.

claims.claim: Idaho allows the property tax reduction if the owner occupies the residential improvements after January 1 but before April 15, and has not claimed another such reduction for the same year.
claims.quotedLanguage: A property tax reduction shall be allowed pursuant to the provisions of sections 63-701 through 63-710, Idaho Code, if the owner occupies the residential improvements after January 1 but before April 15, and if no other property tax reductions or occupancy tax reductions under this section have been claimed by the owner for the same year.
claims.notes: There is a narrow transfer rule for veterans rated 100% disabled who move between April 15 and October 1 (63-702(1)(c)); the page mentions it only as an exception and does not explain it.

claims.claim: The right to file an Idaho property tax reduction claim is personal to the claimant and does not survive the claimant's death, except that a timely claim filed before death is allowed to the personal representative, heirs, or owning trust or entity, among other listed exceptions.
claims.quotedLanguage: The right to file a claim under the provisions of sections 63-701 through 63-710, Idaho Code, shall be personal to the claimant and shall not survive his death except: ... If a claimant dies after having filed a timely claim, the amount thereof shall be allowed to his personal representative, if one is appointed, or to surviving heirs or to the trust or other entity owning the property, as appropriate
claims.notes: There is a further exception for a widow or widower succeeding to an entity-held property (63-702(2)(b)); not described on the page.

claims.claim: Idaho's property tax reduction is allowed on the claimant's homestead for the current year only, and is based on the current year's assessed value and levy.
claims.quotedLanguage: shall be allowed a reduction in taxes on his homestead for the current year only, in the amounts provided by subsection (4) of this section. ... The claimant property owner's tax reduction shall be based upon the current year's assessed value and the current year's levy.

claims.claim: Idaho's property tax reduction ranges from a maximum of $1,500 (or actual taxes, if less) at the lowest income limit down to $250 at the highest, and a home whose current assessed value exceeds the greater of $400,000 or 200% of the county median for exempt homes is referred to the property tax deferral program instead (with an exception for 100%-disabled veterans).
claims.quotedLanguage: The lowest income limitation shall allow a maximum reduction of one thousand five hundred dollars ($1,500) in tax year 2021 and thereafter or actual property taxes or occupancy taxes, as applicable, whichever is less. Each income limitation and reduction amount shall be prorated based on the basic maximum reduction, in practicable increments, so that the highest income limitation will provide for a reduction of two hundred fifty dollars ($250) or actual property taxes, whichever is less. ... if the current year's assessed value of the home owned by the individual, according to the current year's assessment notice, exceeds the greater of four hundred thousand dollars ($400,000) or two hundred percent (200%) of the median assessed valuation for all homes in the county receiving the homestead exemption pursuant to section 63-602G, Idaho Code, then the individual will instead be referred to the property tax deferral program set forth in sections 63-712 through 63-721, Idaho Code.
claims.notes: Ada's median figure is not stated anywhere read for this page — never compute or state Ada's threshold. The Ada Assessor independently says 'by as much as $1,500'.

claims.claim: The Ada County Assessor says Property Tax Reduction applications must be received between January 1 and April 15, that applicants must apply every year, and that an approved reduction appears on the December tax bill.
claims.quotedLanguage: Applications must be received between January 1 and April 15*. ... If your application is approved, your property tax reduction will appear on your December tax bill. ... Applicants must apply every year.
claims.notes: The asterisk is the county's: a weekend/holiday April 15 rolls to the next business day.

claims.claim: An Idaho property tax deferral ends on a sale or other transfer of title to any part of the property (except to a surviving spouse of a deceased qualified claimant), and any unpaid deferred tax and interest must then be paid to the State Tax Commission within 180 days.
claims.quotedLanguage: A sale or other transfer of title to the property or any part of the property except a transfer of title to a surviving spouse of a deceased qualified claimant; ... When a deferral of property tax is terminated any unpaid amount of deferred tax and interest shall be paid to the state tax commission no later than one hundred eighty (180) days after the termination.
claims.notes: Deferral also terminates on the death of the last qualified claimant and when the property stops qualifying for the 63-602G exemption. The page does not say how a title company handles a deferral lien at closing — not sourced.

claims.claim: Deferred Idaho property taxes accrue interest and remain a lien on the property; the State Tax Commission records a notice of lien with the county recorder, and that lien takes priority from its filing rather than as a first and prior lien.
claims.quotedLanguage: The lien imposed by section 63-206, Idaho Code, shall continue to be a lien on the property in the amount of deferred taxes and interest thereon. The state tax commission shall file with the county recorder of the county in which the property is located a notice of lien for deferred property taxes. ... the lien for deferred taxes and interest shall not be a first and prior lien but shall take its priority from the date and time of filing of the notice of lien.

claims.claim: Idaho requires the valuation assessment notice to be delivered or mailed by the first Monday in June, and the notice must state the current market value for assessment purposes, the right to appeal to the county board of equalization, and the previous two years' values and taxes.
claims.quotedLanguage: mailed to the taxpayer or to his agent or representative at his last known post office address no later than the first Monday in June. ... The notice shall, in clear terms, inform the taxpayer of the market value for assessment purposes of the taxpayer's property for the current year and the right to appeal to the county board of equalization. The notice shall also state: ... The market value for assessment purposes of the taxpayer's property for the previous two (2) years; ... The property taxes on the taxpayer's property by each taxing district and unit for the previous two (2) years;
claims.notes: ⚠️ The section page displays TWO versions: one marked '[EFFECTIVE UNTIL JANUARY 1, 2024]' and one '[effective january 1, 2024]'. Only the latter is current; every quote here is from it. ⚠️ DISCREPANCY: for the subsequent roll the statute says notices go out 'not later than the third Monday in November'; the Ada Assessor's appeals page says 'no later than the fourth Monday in November'. The page does not state the subsequent-roll notice date.

claims.claim: An Idaho taxpayer may appeal an assessment or exemption decision to the county board of equalization in writing; an appeal of an assessment on the property roll must be filed by the end of the county's normal business hours on the fourth Monday of June, and the board may consider only timely appeals.
claims.quotedLanguage: Taxpayers may file an appeal of an assessment or exemption decision with the county board of equalization. An appeal shall be made in writing on a form provided by the county board of equalization or assessor and must identify the taxpayer, the property which is the subject of the appeal and the reason for the appeal. An appeal of an assessment listed on the property roll must be filed on or before the end of the county's normal business hours on the fourth Monday of June. ... The board of equalization may consider an appeal only if it is timely filed.

claims.claim: Before an Idaho county board of equalization the taxpayer bears the burden of proving the assessor's determination wrong, and a preponderance of the evidence suffices.
claims.quotedLanguage: The taxpayer shall have the burden of proof in seeking affirmative relief to establish that the determination of the assessor is erroneous, including any determination of assessed value. A preponderance of the evidence shall suffice to sustain the burden of proof.
claims.notes: ⚠️ DISCREPANCY: the Ada Assessor's appeals page quotes a standard of 'clear and convincing evidence' (unattributed quotation). 63-502 as displayed says preponderance suffices for the board. The page cites the statute only. A reviewer may want to check whether the county's quote comes from the 63-511 appeal stage; not read here.

claims.claim: The Ada County Assessor says board of equalization appeals address only market value, not taxes, and completed forms must be filed with the Ada County Commissioner's Office by 5:00 p.m. on the fourth Monday of June.
claims.quotedLanguage: The appeal will only address the market value of your property. An appeal to the Board is not a forum to protest property taxes. ... Completed forms must be filed with the Ada County Commissioner’s Office on or before the 4th Monday of June at 5:00 p.m.

claims.claim: The Ada County Assessor says owners can view and download their assessment notices from the Assessor's online property records, and that the appraiser will consider market evidence an owner submits.
claims.quotedLanguage: Property owners may view and download copies of their assessment notices from the Assessor's Online Property Records page. ... The appraiser assigned to assess your property will consider any evidence you wish to submit.

claims.claim: Under Idaho Code 45-1506(12), the grantor, a successor in interest, or a subordinate lienholder may, at any time within 115 days of the recording of the notice of default, pay the beneficiary the entire amount then due under the deed of trust, other than principal that would not be due had no default occurred, and so cure the default.
claims.quotedLanguage: the grantor or his successor in interest in the trust property or any part thereof, or any beneficiary under a subordinate deed of trust or any person having a subordinate lien or encumbrance of record thereon, at any time within one hundred fifteen (115) days of the recording of the notice of default under such deed of trust, if the power of sale therein is to be exercised, or otherwise at any time prior to the entry of a decree of foreclosure, may pay to the beneficiary or their successors in interest, respectively, the entire amount then due under the terms of the deed of trust and the obligation secured thereby ... other than such portion of the principal as would not then be due had no default occurred, and thereby cure the default theretofore existing
claims.notes: TRAP: the 115 days run from the RECORDING OF THE NOTICE OF DEFAULT, not from the notice of sale and not from the first missed payment. Do not subtract it from the 120-day sale notice in id-trustee-sale-120-day-notice; the two periods start from different events. Where foreclosure is judicial the statute's alternative is 'prior to the entry of a decree of foreclosure'. Never tell a reader what their own cure date is.

claims.claim: When a default is cured under Idaho Code 45-1506(12), all foreclosure proceedings are to be dismissed or discontinued and the obligation and deed of trust are reinstated as if no acceleration had occurred.
claims.quotedLanguage: and thereupon, all proceedings theretofore had or instituted shall be dismissed or discontinued and the obligation and deed of trust shall be reinstated and shall be and remain in force and effect, the same as if no acceleration had occurred.
claims.notes: Must be stated together with af-cure-within-115-days (the time limit) and af-cure-amount-includes-costs (the amount).

claims.claim: The amount needed to cure under Idaho Code 45-1506(12) includes costs and expenses actually incurred in enforcing the obligation, a reasonable trustee's fee limited by 45-1502(6), and attorney's fees as the promissory note may provide.
claims.quotedLanguage: including costs and expenses actually incurred in enforcing the terms of such obligation and a reasonable trustee's fee subject to the limitations imposed by subsection (6) of section 45-1502, Idaho Code, and attorney's fees as may be provided in the promissory note
claims.notes: The cure figure is more than the missed payments. 45-1502(6) was NOT read for this page; do not state the trustee's fee limit.

claims.claim: Under Idaho Code 45-1506(10), the trustee's deed conveys to the purchaser at the trustee's sale the interest in the property that the grantor had, or had the power to convey, when the trust deed was signed, together with any interest acquired afterwards.
claims.quotedLanguage: The trustee's deed shall convey to the purchaser the interest in the property which the grantor had, or had the power to convey, at the time of the execution by him of the trust deed together with any interest the grantor or his successors in interest acquired after the execution of such trust deed.
claims.notes: Used only to support the plain point that the owner's own sale has to close before the trustee's sale. Finality and redemption (45-1508) belong to the after-sale guide and were not read here.

claims.claim: Idaho Code 45-1506C requires a supplemental notice to accompany the notice of default where the loan was made by a state or federally regulated beneficiary and is a noncommercial loan secured by a deed of trust on the borrower's primary residence; a property granted the homeowner's property tax exemption for the year the notice of default is recorded is deemed the primary residence, and if no exemption was granted for that year the section does not apply.
claims.quotedLanguage: In the case of a loan made by a state or federally regulated beneficiary, which loan is secured by a deed of trust encumbering a borrower's primary residential property for any noncommercial loan, the notice provided in this section shall accompany the notice of default provided to the grantor. The beneficiary or its agent shall determine whether the subject real property is a borrower's primary residence by searching the county assessor's tax rolls prior to recording a notice of default to confirm whether such real property has been granted a homeowner's property tax exemption pursuant to section 63-602G, Idaho Code. Any property for which a homeowner's property tax exemption has been granted for the year in which the notice of default is recorded shall be deemed to be a borrower's primary residential dwelling. If no homeowner's property tax exemption has been granted for the year in which the notice of default is recorded, the provisions of this section shall not apply.
claims.notes: TRAP: the whole section turns on the homeowner's exemption (63-602G) being in place for the year the notice of default is recorded. A rental, a second home, or a home whose exemption lapsed is outside it. Never tell a reader the section applies to them.

claims.claim: The statutory form of the 45-1506C notice tells the borrower that the beneficiary can provide the exact amount owed but the borrower has to ask, by calling a toll-free number or sending a written request by certified mail.
claims.quotedLanguage: The beneficiary can provide you with the exact amount that you owe, but you have to ask. Call (enter the toll-free telephone number) to find out the exact amount you must pay to bring your mortgage loan current and to obtain other details about your loan. You also can send a written request for this information by certified mail
claims.notes: This is wording of the notice form, which must 'substantially conform'. Attribute it to the notice.

claims.claim: The 45-1506C notice tells a borrower who cannot afford the current payments to contact the beneficiary immediately about loss mitigation programs, states that the borrower may or may not qualify for a loan modification or other alternative to foreclosure, and says the borrower may request a meeting with the beneficiary.
claims.quotedLanguage: you need to contact the beneficiary immediately to ask about any available loss mitigation programs. You may or may not qualify for a loan modification or other alternative to foreclosure. You may request to meet with the beneficiary to discuss options for modifying your loan.
claims.notes: The section creates a right to ask and to be answered, not a right to a modification. Always carry the 'may or may not qualify' half.

claims.claim: Under the 45-1506C notice, a borrower who wants to apply for a loan modification must complete and return the enclosed modification request form by certified mail, return receipt requested, and the beneficiary must receive it on or before a date that is 30 days after the date of the notice.
claims.quotedLanguage: IF YOU WANT TO APPLY FOR A MODIFICATION OF YOUR LOAN, YOU MUST COMPLETE AND RETURN THE ENCLOSED "MODIFICATION REQUEST FORM" BY CERTIFIED MAIL, RETURN RECEIPT REQUESTED. THE BENEFICIARY MUST RECEIVE THE FORM ON OR BEFORE (enter the date), WHICH IS THIRTY (30) DAYS AFTER THE DATE BELOW.
claims.notes: TRAP: RECEIVED by the beneficiary within 30 days of the date on the notice, not postmarked. Certified mail, return receipt requested. The actual deadline is the date printed on the borrower's own notice.

claims.claim: If the grantor returns the 45-1506C form by the date on it, the beneficiary must evaluate the request and notify the grantor in writing, not later than 45 days after receiving the form, whether it approves or denies the request or needs more information; a trustee's sale may not occur until after the beneficiary timely responds.
claims.quotedLanguage: If a grantor returns the form identified in subsection (2) of this section to the beneficiary by the date specified on the form, the beneficiary or the beneficiary's agent shall review the information the grantor provided in the form and shall evaluate the grantor's request. The beneficiary or the beneficiary's agent, as soon as reasonably practicable but not later than forty-five (45) days after receiving the form, shall notify the grantor in writing whether the beneficiary approves or denies the request or requires additional information. A trustee's sale for the property subject to the loan may not occur until after the beneficiary or the beneficiary's agent timely responds to the grantor.
claims.notes: The bar on the trustee's sale lasts only until the beneficiary responds. It is not a stay of foreclosure and a denial ends it. Depends on the form having been returned on time.

claims.claim: If the grantor timely requests a meeting, Idaho Code 45-1506C(4) requires the beneficiary or its agent to meet in person or speak by telephone before responding to the modification request, and the person who meets must have or be able to obtain authority to modify the loan; the beneficiary is treated as complying if, within seven business days after it attempts contact, the grantor does not schedule a meeting or fails to attend.
claims.quotedLanguage: if the grantor timely requests a meeting with the beneficiary, the beneficiary or the beneficiary's agent shall either meet with the grantor in person or speak to the grantor by telephone before the beneficiary or the beneficiary's agent responds to the grantor's request to modify the loan. ... within seven (7) business days after the beneficiary or the beneficiary's agent attempts to contact the grantor, the grantor does not schedule a meeting, or fails to attend a scheduled meeting or telephone call. ... The beneficiary or the beneficiary's agent that meets with the grantor shall have or be able to obtain authority to modify the loan.
claims.notes: State the seven-business-day point with it: a borrower who does not schedule or attend loses the meeting.

claims.claim: The 45-1506C notice carries a warning: never pay someone to help obtain a loan modification, and help is available for free from housing counselors certified through HUD, with a current list of certified counselors in Idaho on HUD's website.
claims.quotedLanguage: WARNING: You may get offers from people who tell you they can help you keep your property. Never pay someone to help you obtain a loan modification. Help is available for free from housing counselors who are certified through the department of housing and urban development (HUD). Visit the HUD website for a current list of certified housing counselors in Idaho.
claims.notes: Idaho's own statutory wording. We are among the 'people who tell you they can help'; quote it straight.

claims.claim: The federal early-intervention and loss-mitigation procedures in 12 CFR 1024.39 through 1024.41 apply only to a mortgage loan secured by the borrower's principal residence, and, except as 1024.41(j) provides, sections 1024.38 through 1024.41 do not apply to small servicers, to reverse mortgage transactions, or to certain qualified lenders.
claims.quotedLanguage: Except as otherwise provided in § 1024.41(j), §§ 1024.38 through 1024.41 of this subpart shall not apply to the following: ... A servicer that qualifies as a small servicer pursuant to 12 CFR 1026.41(e)(4); ... The procedures set forth in §§ 1024.39 through 1024.41 of this subpart only apply to a mortgage loan that is secured by a property that is a borrower's principal residence.
claims.notes: The small-servicer definition (12 CFR 1026.41(e)(4)) was NOT read. Say 'small servicers' without defining them. Small servicers remain subject to the 120-day rule through 1024.41(j): see af-regx-small-servicer.

claims.claim: Under 12 CFR 1024.41(j), a small servicer is still subject to the 120-day prohibition on foreclosure referral and may not start or complete a foreclosure while a borrower is performing under a loss mitigation agreement.
claims.quotedLanguage: A small servicer shall be subject to the prohibition on foreclosure referral in paragraph (f)(1) of this section. A small servicer shall not make the first notice or filing required by applicable law for any judicial or non-judicial foreclosure process and shall not move for foreclosure judgment or order of sale, or conduct a foreclosure sale, if a borrower is performing pursuant to the terms of an agreement on a loss mitigation option.
claims.notes: Pairs with af-regx-scope.

claims.claim: Under 12 CFR 1024.39(a), a servicer must establish or make good faith efforts to establish live contact with a delinquent borrower no later than the 36th day of delinquency and, promptly after contact, inform the borrower about the availability of loss mitigation options, if appropriate.
claims.quotedLanguage: a servicer shall establish or make good faith efforts to establish live contact with a delinquent borrower no later than the 36th day of a borrower's delinquency and again no later than 36 days after each payment due date so long as the borrower remains delinquent. Promptly after establishing live contact with a borrower, the servicer shall inform the borrower about the availability of loss mitigation options, if appropriate.
claims.notes: Applies only within the scope set by 12 CFR 1024.30 (principal residence; small servicers and some others exempt): state with af-regx-scope. Federal rule, enforced against the servicer; never tell a reader their servicer violated it. Bankruptcy and FDCPA exemptions in 1024.39(c)-(d) exist and are not described.

claims.claim: Under 12 CFR 1024.39(b), a servicer must send a delinquent borrower a written notice no later than the 45th day of delinquency that encourages the borrower to contact the servicer, gives the servicer's telephone number and mailing address, and gives the website for the CFPB or HUD list of homeownership counselors and HUD's toll-free number.
claims.quotedLanguage: a servicer shall provide to a delinquent borrower a written notice with the information set forth in paragraph (b)(2) of this section no later than the 45th day of the borrower's delinquency ... A statement encouraging the borrower to contact the servicer; ... The Web site to access either the Bureau list or the HUD list of homeownership counselors or counseling organizations, and the HUD toll-free telephone number to access homeownership counselors or counseling organizations.
claims.notes: Applies only within the scope set by 12 CFR 1024.30 (principal residence; small servicers and some others exempt): state with af-regx-scope. Federal rule, enforced against the servicer; never tell a reader their servicer violated it. The notice need not be sent more than once in any 180-day period.

claims.claim: Under 12 CFR 1024.41(f)(1), a servicer may not make the first notice or filing required by applicable law for a judicial or non-judicial foreclosure unless the loan is more than 120 days delinquent, the foreclosure is based on a due-on-sale violation, or the servicer is joining another lienholder's foreclosure.
claims.quotedLanguage: A servicer shall not make the first notice or filing required by applicable law for any judicial or non-judicial foreclosure process unless: ... A borrower's mortgage loan obligation is more than 120 days delinquent; ... The foreclosure is based on a borrower's violation of a due-on-sale clause; or ... The servicer is joining the foreclosure action of a superior or subordinate lienholder.
claims.notes: TRAP: this federal 120 days (delinquency before the first filing) is a DIFFERENT period from Idaho's 120-day notice of sale (id-trustee-sale-120-day-notice). Never merge them or add them into a total. Which Idaho document counts as the 'first notice or filing' is not stated in the rule text read here; do not name it. Applies only within the scope set by 12 CFR 1024.30 (principal residence; small servicers and some others exempt): state with af-regx-scope. Federal rule, enforced against the servicer; never tell a reader their servicer violated it.

claims.claim: 12 CFR 1024.41(a) states that nothing in the section imposes a duty on a servicer to provide any borrower with any specific loss mitigation option.
claims.quotedLanguage: Nothing in § 1024.41 imposes a duty on a servicer to provide any borrower with any specific loss mitigation option.
claims.notes: The honesty anchor for the federal section: the rule governs procedure and timing, not outcomes. Must accompany any description of the application protections.

claims.claim: Under 12 CFR 1024.41(b)(2), a servicer that receives a loss mitigation application 45 days or more before a foreclosure sale must tell the borrower in writing, within 5 days excluding legal public holidays, Saturdays and Sundays, whether the application is complete or incomplete, and if incomplete what additional documents and information are needed.
claims.quotedLanguage: If a servicer receives a loss mitigation application 45 days or more before a foreclosure sale, a servicer shall: ... Notify the borrower in writing within 5 days (excluding legal public holidays, Saturdays, and Sundays) after receiving the loss mitigation application that the servicer acknowledges receipt of the loss mitigation application and that the servicer has determined that the loss mitigation application is either complete or incomplete. If a loss mitigation application is incomplete, the notice shall state the additional documents and information the borrower must submit to make the loss mitigation application complete
claims.notes: Applies only within the scope set by 12 CFR 1024.30 (principal residence; small servicers and some others exempt): state with af-regx-scope. Federal rule, enforced against the servicer; never tell a reader their servicer violated it.

claims.claim: Under 12 CFR 1024.41(c)(1), a servicer that receives a complete loss mitigation application more than 37 days before a foreclosure sale must, within 30 days, evaluate the borrower for all loss mitigation options available to the borrower and give written notice of which options, if any, it will offer.
claims.quotedLanguage: if a servicer receives a complete loss mitigation application more than 37 days before a foreclosure sale, then, within 30 days of receiving the complete loss mitigation application, a servicer shall: ... Evaluate the borrower for all loss mitigation options available to the borrower; and ... Provide the borrower with a notice in writing stating the servicer's determination of which loss mitigation options, if any, it will offer to the borrower on behalf of the owner or assignee of the mortgage.
claims.notes: 'Complete' is defined in 1024.41(b)(1) as the servicer having received all the information it requires. An incomplete application does not trigger this. Applies only within the scope set by 12 CFR 1024.30 (principal residence; small servicers and some others exempt): state with af-regx-scope. Federal rule, enforced against the servicer; never tell a reader their servicer violated it.

claims.claim: Under 12 CFR 1024.41(f)(2), if a borrower submits a complete loss mitigation application before the servicer has made the first foreclosure notice or filing, the servicer may not make that notice or filing unless it has told the borrower in writing that the borrower is not eligible for any option and any appeal is exhausted or unavailable, the borrower rejects all options offered, or the borrower fails to perform under a loss mitigation agreement.
claims.quotedLanguage: If a borrower submits a complete loss mitigation application during the pre-foreclosure review period set forth in paragraph (f)(1) of this section or before a servicer has made the first notice or filing required by applicable law for any judicial or non-judicial foreclosure process, a servicer shall not make the first notice or filing required by applicable law for any judicial or non-judicial foreclosure process unless: ... The borrower rejects all loss mitigation options offered by the servicer; or ... The borrower fails to perform under an agreement on a loss mitigation option.
claims.notes: Applies only within the scope set by 12 CFR 1024.30 (principal residence; small servicers and some others exempt): state with af-regx-scope. Federal rule, enforced against the servicer; never tell a reader their servicer violated it.

claims.claim: Under 12 CFR 1024.41(g), if a borrower submits a complete loss mitigation application after the foreclosure has started but more than 37 days before a foreclosure sale, the servicer may not move for a foreclosure judgment or order of sale, or conduct a foreclosure sale, unless the borrower has been found ineligible with any appeal exhausted or unavailable, rejects all options offered, or fails to perform under a loss mitigation agreement.
claims.quotedLanguage: If a borrower submits a complete loss mitigation application after a servicer has made the first notice or filing required by applicable law for any judicial or non-judicial foreclosure process but more than 37 days before a foreclosure sale, a servicer shall not move for foreclosure judgment or order of sale, or conduct a foreclosure sale, unless:
claims.notes: TRAP: 'more than 37 days before a foreclosure sale' and 'complete'. An application inside 37 days, or an incomplete one, does not get this protection under the text read. Never write that applying 'stops' a foreclosure. The three exceptions are quoted in af-regx-application-before-referral's parallel list at (f)(2); (g)(1)-(3) repeat them. Applies only within the scope set by 12 CFR 1024.30 (principal residence; small servicers and some others exempt): state with af-regx-scope. Federal rule, enforced against the servicer; never tell a reader their servicer violated it.

claims.claim: Under 12 CFR 1024.41(h), where a complete application was received 90 days or more before a foreclosure sale, the servicer must let the borrower appeal a denial of any loan modification program, the borrower has 14 days to appeal, the appeal must be reviewed by different personnel, and the servicer must give its determination within 30 days; that determination is not subject to further appeal.
